approachQuestion.prompt:
Even-share batches. Count nonempty contiguous intervals whose signed total is divisible by positive k. Return one count.

Input: a=[2,-1,2], k=3. Output: 1.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200000; 1 ≤ k ≤ 200000; -1000000 ≤ a[i] ≤ 1000000. Normalize remainders into 0..k-1. Counts fit 64 bits.

Which approach handles the complete task correctly and efficiently?

options.text: Allocate k zero counters and seed counter[0]=1. Maintain the normalized running remainder; add its previous frequency to the answer, then increment that counter.
options.feedback: Two boundaries have equal normalized remainders exactly when their difference is divisible by k. Querying first excludes empty intervals.

options.text: Count only boundaries whose running remainder is zero.
options.feedback: For [1,3] and k=3, the valid interval [3] starts after a nonzero remainder and is missed.

options.text: Enumerate all intervals, compute each total incrementally and test divisibility.
options.feedback: This gives correct results, but repeatedly traverses overlapping candidates. The selected summary reuses their shared work.

feedback.reason: Allocate k zero counters and seed counter[0]=1. Maintain the normalized running remainder; add its previous frequency to the answer, then increment that counter.
details: Allocate k zero counters and seed counter[0]=1. Maintain the normalized running remainder; add its previous frequency to the answer, then increment that counter.
Equal normalized remainders imply their prefix difference is divisible by k. Normalize negative sums into the same residue classes. Seed remainder zero to count intervals starting at the beginning.

“Allocate k zero counters and seed counter[0]=1. Maintain the normalized running remainder; add its previous frequency to the answer, then increment that counter.”: Two boundaries have equal normalized remainders exactly when their difference is divisible by k. Querying first excludes empty intervals.
“Count only boundaries whose running remainder is zero.”: For [1,3] and k=3, the valid interval [3] starts after a nonzero remainder and is missed.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the method in the reveal. Choose its tightest worst-case time and worst-case auxiliary-space pair. Use constant-time 64-bit arithmetic. Exclude read-only input and required output; include every described table. All loops are iterative, with no recursive stack or input copies.

options.text: O(n + k) time; O(k) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Include initialization of k residue counters before the n-entry scan.
details: Zeroing k counters costs O(k); the scan costs O(n). The dense counter array occupies O(k) space.
Use constant-time 64-bit arithmetic. Exclude read-only input and required output; include every described table. All loops are iterative, with no recursive stack or input copies.

There are k initialization writes followed by n iterations, each doing fixed 64-bit arithmetic, one indexed frequency read, and one increment. Add these phases to obtain O(n+k). The scan neither enumerates all intervals, as an O(n²) approach would, nor scans all k counters per entry, as O(nk) would suggest. Because k is an independent input parameter, an n-only time bound also omits potentially dominant initialization.

The k dense counters remain live throughout the scan; the remainder, answer, and index add only constant state. Hence auxiliary space is O(k). The O(n)-time/O(1)-space option omits both counter initialization and the actual array. The supplied input and returned scalar count are excluded, but the frequency array is neither of them.
